There's a real essay underneath this, and the first thing worth saying is that you already did the hard part. You took a position, you held it across five paragraphs, and you went out and found outside support instead of just insisting. The CDC statistics are specific and checkable, and going to a named researcher who actually studies adolescent sleep is a better instinct than a lot of drafts show.

### What's working
The structure is clean and easy to follow, the paragraphs stay on their topics, and you took the trouble to acknowledge the other side, which plenty of writers skip entirely.

### Places you could push
Your thesis, "Schools should start later in the morning because it would be better for students in a lot of ways", makes a promise without telling us what's inside it. Readers relax when they know what's coming. One possible version: "Schools should start later because teenagers cannot fall asleep as early as the schedule assumes they can, and because the cost of leaving the schedule alone falls entirely on students." Only keep that if it sounds like you.

Your second paragraph has your strongest evidence, and its last sentence, "Sleep is very important for teenagers", is the spot where you get to tell us what all those numbers prove. Right now it repeats them instead.

The paragraph about Dr. Carskadon explains her work clearly and respectfully. I'd love one more sentence at the end of it linking the phase delay to the actual start time.

Writing a counterargument at all takes some nerve. "eventually people get used to it" is being asked to do the entire job of answering, though, and it could use company.

Your transitions are easy to follow. If you wanted them working harder, they could name relationships instead of order.

And a small one: give the commas in the CDC sentence a second look.

None of that changes the fact that the bones are good here. Which of these feels most doable to you? If there's a rubric or a comment from your teacher, tell me what it says, and I can point at the one that matters most instead of listing all of them.

000|dense.md: Read as a whole, this is a competent five-paragraph argumentative essay that does most of what the form asks of it: it takes a position, holds it, supports it with outside sources rather than personal opinion, acknowledges an opposing view, and closes by returning to the claim. That is more than many drafts manage, and the sourcing in particular is real, since the CDC figures are specific and the Carskadon material is exactly the research a reader would want to see cited here. The difficulties are mostly in the joints. The thesis, "Schools should start later in the morning because it would be better for students in a lot of ways", commits to a position but not to any reason for it, which leaves the three body paragraphs free to arrive in any order and leaves a reader without a map; naming two or three actual reasons in that sentence would also hand you your topic sentences for free. In the second paragraph the evidence is strong and the closing sentence, "Sleep is very important for teenagers", restates the sources rather than drawing anything out of them, so the paragraph proves that teenagers are underslept without ever proving that the school schedule is the thing to change. The third paragraph has a related problem in a different costume, in that it is largely a biography of the researcher, and while the phase-delay finding is reported accurately, nothing is done with it, so a reader who fully accepts that adolescent body clocks shift can still leave the paragraph unconvinced that first bell should move. The counterargument paragraph is worth keeping and needs something real underneath it, since "eventually people get used to it" grants the objection about buses and sports and then declines to answer it; districts that have moved their start times have published what it actually cost them, and one sentence of that would outweigh the three currently there. Smaller matters: the transitions announce sequence rather than relationship, the second sentence of the introduction is warm-up, and the conventions are clean enough that I would leave them alone. If you can tell me what rubric this is being scored against and how much time you have before it is due, I can tell you which of those is worth the evening and which is worth ten minutes.

001|coach.md:
Before anything else: this draft has the two things that are hardest to teach, which are a position you're willing to hold and evidence you actually went and got. Everything below is refinement, not rescue.

The place I'd start, gently, is the warrant, the sentence that says why a piece of evidence proves the point it sits under. Each body paragraph here gives us data and a claim and leaves the connective tissue between them unwritten, which is why the essay feels thinner than its research. Your sleep paragraph closes on "Sleep is very important for teenagers", a restatement occupying the slot where the so-what test gets answered. Treat that final sentence as the paragraph's warrant instead, and name what the CDC figures license you to conclude about start times specifically rather than about sleep generally.

The Carskadon paragraph has the same shape plus one extra wrinkle. The term "phase delay" arrives as a dropped quotation: a signal phrase introduces it, and then nothing unpacks it or returns to it. The quote sandwich you want is quotation, then paraphrase in your own words, then the causal mechanism it implies, which is that melatonin onset shifts later, sleep debt accumulates, and first period lands inside the biological night. That last part is the paragraph's real topic sentence, and right now it isn't written anywhere.

Your fourth paragraph is braver than most, so let me be careful here: what it contains is a concession without a rebuttal underneath it, and "eventually people get used to it" is a qualifier being asked to do a rebuttal's job. One sentence of backing from a district that has already done this would move it from polite to persuasive.

Two smaller things, offered lightly. The openings "One reason", "Another reason" and "Some people say" are sequence markers rather than logical connectives, so the essay reads as a list of reasons instead of a line of reasoning. And your ending is hortatory where it could be operationalized: nothing in the draft says what "better for students" would look like if it happened, or how anyone would know.

Tell me who's reading this and what they're grading, and I'll tell you where to spend the effort. Either way, the exigence is real and you have hold of it.

001|peer.md:
Structurally the essay is intact; rhetorically it is a run of enthymemes with the load-bearing halves left out.

Start with stasis, because the drift begins there. The draft never settles which question it is arguing, whether adolescents are harmed (fact), whether the schedule is what harms them (cause), or whether districts ought to act (policy), and it slides between all three, which is why the evidence keeps arriving without a job to do. The thesis licenses the drift: "because it would be better for students in a lot of ways" is an unqualified good rather than a contestable proposition, and it forecasts no reasons, so the body paragraphs inherit no obligations.

Paragraph two is a clean Toulmin fragment with the warrant excised. Data, the CDC hours and the seven-in-ten figure; claim, implied; and sitting where the warrant belongs, "Sleep is very important for teenagers", which is the data again in evaluative dress. Nothing links sleep debt to bell time, so a reader can grant every fact and decline the conclusion.

Paragraph three is worse in a more interesting way, because the material is better. The phase-delay finding is a dropped quotation: attributive tag, quotation, no unpacking, no backing, no return. The paragraph then substitutes ethos for reasoning, offering tenure and reputation where a causal mechanism belongs, which is argument from authority doing the work an inference should. The finding only becomes an argument once someone writes the sentence saying sleep onset is not volitional and that "go to bed earlier" is therefore not an available remedy.

Four is a concession with no rebuttal. The objection is granted and then dissolved in "But almost any change causes problems at first, and eventually people get used to it", which is a temporal hedge rather than a refutation; no cost comparison, no qualifier narrowing what is conceded, and the burden of proof stays exactly where the opposition left it.

Transitions are ordinal rather than inferential, sequence markers announcing that another item is coming. And the close is hortatory rather than operationalized, with no measurable outcome by which anyone could later judge the policy.

Whose draft is this, and scored against what? The diagnosis doesn't change; the triage does.

001|dense.md: What this draft is missing is not evidence but inference: at every point where a reader needs the writer to say why a fact matters, the essay says something further about the fact instead. The thesis sets the pattern by promising a benefit and naming no reason for it, so the paragraphs that follow are related by topic rather than by any line of reasoning, and each of them presents data with the warrant left unwritten. In the sleep paragraph the CDC figures are well chosen and correctly attributed, and then the closing sentence, "Sleep is very important for teenagers", is a nominalization of the data rather than a conclusion drawn from it; the paragraph never states the causal mechanism that would connect insufficient sleep to the start time in particular, which means a reader can accept every number and still see no reason to move the bell. The Carskadon paragraph repeats the pattern with better material and at greater cost, since the finding enters as a dropped quotation, introduced by a signal phrase and then abandoned, with no paraphrase, no backing, and no consequence drawn; because the paragraph offers credentials where reasoning belongs, it argues from ethos and leaves the strongest available fact unspent. The counterargument fares no better, in that bus schedules and athletics are conceded and then answered by the claim that people adjust, a concession whose rebuttal never arrives, leaving the objection's cost unpriced. Between paragraphs the connective tissue is ordinal, "One reason" and "Another reason" and "Some people say" being sequence markers that carry no inferential load, so the organization is achieved by enumeration and a reader can tell what comes next but not why it follows. The conclusion is hortatory, asking for action in "It is time for schools to do the right thing and let students sleep" without ever operationalizing the outcome, so there is no measurable claim about attendance or grades or crash rates and therefore no way to say afterward whether the policy worked. The prose itself is clean, with a mild taste for expletive constructions of the "It is true that" and "It is time" variety, which subordination would tighten. Whether any of this is worth pursuing depends on what the assignment actually rewards, which I can't see from here.

Since that paragraph holds your best material, here's one way it could go:

"Carskadon's research shows that during puberty the brain's melatonin release shifts about two hours later, which means the sleep teenagers appear to be choosing to lose isn't a choice at all. If sleep onset is biologically delayed and first bell is not, the schedule itself guarantees the deficit. That is a problem no amount of willpower or earlier bedtimes can solve; only a later start can."

Take the idea rather than my sentences. The voice should stay yours, and that last line is the so-what test answered out loud.

Your thesis is upstream of all of it. Taking the rubric at face value: 70 of your 100 points sit on argument and evidence, and both rows are failing for the same reason, which is that every body paragraph stops at the data and never supplies the warrant. That's your teacher's note from last time in technical dress. The phrase "summarizing your sources instead of using them" is the teacher-facing description of a missing warrant, and the essay is a chain of enthymemes because of it.

Two paragraphs rewritten, so you can see the difference structurally instead of taking my word for it.

Paragraph two, ending replaced: "If the CDC's threshold is eight hours and seven in ten students fall below it on school nights, then sleep deprivation here is not an individual failure of discipline but a predictable output of the schedule. A student in bed by eleven and awake at six is doing everything the advice asks and still lands short. The only variable that can move is the bell."

Paragraph three, whole: "Carskadon's work identifies the causal mechanism behind that shortfall. During puberty the circadian phase delays: melatonin onset arrives later, and falling asleep much before eleven becomes physiologically difficult regardless of intention. The implication for policy is direct. If sleep onset cannot be advanced but wake time can be delayed, the only lever a district actually controls is the start time."

Note what changed. The dropped quotation is integrated, the attributive tag survives and the biography doesn't, and each paragraph now ends on an inference rather than a restatement, which is the so-what test satisfied inside the paragraph. The term "phase delay" is doing argumentative work now instead of sitting there as an appositive curiosity.
